Camera translating along its optical axis
Drag to orbit: the frusta are real 3‑D pyramids whose apexes all lie on one straight, level optical axis.
⚠ Figure failed to load

plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single horizontal strip in which one camera is repeated five times in a row on a white ground, with thick red arrows between and around the copies. Each camera is a black wireframe viewing frustum in three-quarter view: a solid black dot marks the projection center at the left, four straight edges spread rightward from it to the corners of a tall rectangle standing for the image plane, and a faint vertical line inside that rectangle marks its midline. All five frusta match in size and orientation, and every one opens toward the right. A red arrow lies on the axis left of the first camera, another sits in each gap between consecutive cameras, and a final one continues past the last camera to the right edge; all arrowheads point right. Because the arrows run in the same direction the frusta face, the strip shows a camera moving straight ahead down its own optical axis, the case in which the sideways velocity components vanish and only the component along the Z-axis is nonzero.

elements: five identical wireframe camera frusta arranged left-to-right along one horizontal optical axis, all opening toward the right
for each frustum: a solid black dot at the projection center (apex) on the left side
for each frustum: four straight black edges radiating right from the apex to the four corners of the image rectangle
for each frustum: the tall upright image-plane rectangle (four black edges) at the wide end
for each frustum: a faint grey vertical midline drawn inside the image rectangle
for each frustum: the far/near vertical edges of the rectangle drawn with slight three-quarter depth offset (near edge bolder, far edge behind)
thick red horizontal arrow entering from the left edge into the first camera's apex
four thick red horizontal arrows, one in each gap between consecutive cameras
one thick red horizontal arrow continuing past the last camera to the right edge
all red arrowheads as solid triangles pointing right
implied common optical axis line passing through every apex
(flow-field view) a single image rectangle seen front-on with its midline and center point
(flow-field view) a grid of projected scene points on the image plane
(flow-field view) radial flow vectors pointing outward from the image center, longer near the edges, near-zero at the focus of expansion
(3-D view, optional) a sparse cloud of static world scene points ahead of the cameras with sight rays to the moving image plane

interactions.label: Fly forward along the optical axis
interactions.teaches: Translating the camera straight down its own viewing direction leaves the frustum's orientation untouched, and the scene points it images slide outward from the image center.

interactions.label: Position along forward path (t)
interactions.teaches: Scrubbing the camera between the five discrete copies shows that only depth Z to the scene changes — the optical axis and the red arrows keep exactly the same direction, so the sideways velocity components stay zero.

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: The same rightward motion of the frustum in 3-D becomes a purely radial, outward expanding vector field in the image — forward translation produces a focus of expansion at the image center.
Rotating the strip confirms the frusta are genuine 3-D pyramids sharing one straight optical axis rather than flat icons, and that the motion arrows lie exactly on that axis.

demo_steps.title: The camera strip at rest
demo_steps.narration: Five copies of the same camera stand in a row, each apex on the left and each image plane on the right; all frusta face the same way down one optical axis.

demo_steps.title: Stepping forward
demo_steps.narration: Advance the slider: the active camera slides rightward from copy to copy, following the red arrows. Its orientation never changes — only its distance to the scene.

demo_steps.title: End of the path
demo_steps.narration: At the last copy the camera is nearest the scene. The red arrow continues past it, showing the motion is pure translation along +Z with no rotation and no sideways component.

demo_steps.title: What the image sees
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the image plane: the same forward motion shows up as vectors expanding radially outward from the image center, zero at the focus of expansion and largest at the periphery.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World axes: +X is screen-right (the common optical axis and direction of travel), +Y screen-up, +Z the receding three-quarter diagonal. One camera frustum: apex (projection center) at local origin, drawn as a black sphere of radius 0.10; image rectangle at x = +1.30, sized 1.60 (Y, tall) x 1.00 (Z, deep) so it reads clearly taller than wide, exactly as in the source. Four black edges of tube radius ~0.02 connect the apex to the rectangle's four corners; the rectangle's own four edges are the same weight. A single faint grey (#808080) vertical line of the same radius runs top-to-bottom at the rectangle's mid-depth (z = 0). Five identical, unscaled copies with apexes at x = 0, 3.2, 6.4, 9.6, 12.8, all y = z = 0, all opening toward +X — no size taper of any kind between copies. Red motion arrows (#FF0000, shaft radius 0.075, conical head length 0.35, head radius 0.17) lie exactly on the y=z=0 axis, all pointing +X: one entering from x = -2.4 to -0.25 (just before the first apex), one in each of the four gaps spanning from just right of a rectangle (x ≈ previous apex + 1.45) to just left of the next apex (next apex - 0.25), and a final one from x = 14.3 out to x = 16.6 past the last camera. Background white; wireframe black #000000. Flow-field view: the same image rectangle drawn front-on (1.60 tall x 1.20 wide on screen), a 5x5 grid of projected scene points, and red arrows at each point along the radial direction from the image center, with magnitude |v| = |p| * (Tz / Z) so the vector length grows linearly with distance from the center and vanishes exactly at the focus of expansion at the rectangle's midline center. Image-plane velocity model: u = (-Tx + x*Tz)/Z, v = (-Ty + y*Tz)/Z with Tx = Ty = 0, Tz > 0, Z ≈ 6 world units to the scene.
interactionPlan.notes: Build one frustum as a reusable THREE.Group (sphere apex + 8 cylinder/TubeGeometry edges + grey midline) and instance it five times so all copies are provably identical. Use MeshBasicMaterial or thick LineSegments (Line2/LineMaterial with linewidth ~3px) for the crisp constant-width black wireframe look of the source. Red arrows via ArrowHelper replacements built from a cylinder shaft + cone head so their thickness is world-space and consistent. The slider and animation drive the same underlying t parameter (0-4 in copy units); the animation just auto-advances t and loops back. On toggle to the flow-field view, cross-fade: dolly the camera to a front-on orthographic look at a single image rectangle, hide the strip, and fade in the radial arrow field, recomputing arrow lengths from the current t (closer scene = longer vectors). Keep an orthographic-feeling axonometric camera (OrthographicCamera or a long-focal PerspectiveCamera) so the five copies do not perspectively shrink toward the right.  Orbit via OrbitControls with damping, target at the strip center (x ≈ 6.4).

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Animation for advancing the camera copies along their optical axis; the frustum moves straight through the scene while projected points expand from the image center, linking forward Z translation to radial optical flow.
- Slider for time along the forward path; the active camera position and red direction arrows update together, showing that orientation stays fixed while depth to the scene changes.

authoredContext:
For a camera moving forward, as illustrated in
the figure, note that $V_X = V_Y = 0$. In this
case, the motion is only along the $Z$-axis, $V_Z \neq 0$.

Camera moving forward, along the camera axis.

discrepancies: Composition/viewpoint: the source shows the five frusta in a strictly horizontal left-to-right strip filling the frame; the generated strip recedes diagonally down-right and occupies only a small part of the canvas, so the 'row of cameras along one axis' reads much less clearly.
An extra blue 'active' camera is superimposed on the first black frustum at t = 0, producing a doubled/ghosted first camera that has no counterpart in the source.

The source image is completely unlabelled; the generated view adds several red/black text annotations ('optical axis — direction of travel', 'projection centre C', 'image plane', 'T = (0,0,Tz)') that overlap the first frustum and the first red arrow, cluttering the region the source keeps clean.
Frusta are rendered noticeably smaller relative to the arrows than in the source, where each frustum is a dominant element roughly as tall as the arrow gaps are long.
A faint grey optical-axis line is drawn through the whole strip; the source has no such continuous line — only the discrete red arrow segments.
evaluation.notes: Correct primitives (apex dot, four apex edges, image rectangle with grey midline, red axial arrows) and a rich, functional interaction set (mode toggle, slider, play loop, ray/annotation toggles, stepped narration), but the strip is oriented diagonally and rendered small rather than as the source's wide horizontal row, and an overlapping blue duplicate camera plus dense annotations clutter the left end.
action_items: Re-frame the default view so the camera row runs roughly horizontally across the canvas (small azimuth so +X maps near screen-right) and increase zoom so the five frusta fill the frame like the source.
Hide or offset the blue 'active' camera at t = 0 (or start it mid-path) so it does not double up with the first black frustum.
Reposition the 'optical axis', 'projection centre C' and 'image plane' labels with leader offsets that clear the first frustum and the leading red arrow.

Enlarge the frusta relative to the arrow spacing to match the source's proportions, and consider dropping the continuous grey axis line (or making it a dashed annotation only when Annotations is checked).
plan_action_items: Specify axis_screen_angles that keep the translation axis near screen-horizontal, as in the source's near-elevation axonometric drawing.

feedback.rationale: The concept and primitives are correct; the issues are execution-level (camera framing/zoom, duplicate active frustum at t=0, label placement, frustum scale, stray axis line) that can be fixed in rendering.

discrepancies: The camera strip runs diagonally downward across the canvas (axisScreenAngles x:6°) whereas the source lays the five frusta and arrows on one perfectly horizontal baseline; the resulting apparent staircase slightly weakens the 'single straight optical axis' read.

The source figure carries no text at all; the generated view adds several annotation labels, a dashed axis, leader lines and a readout panel. The red 'T = (0, 0, T_z) in camera coords' label lands directly on top of the second red arrow, cluttering the region.

Frusta in the source are drawn with the apex-to-corner diagonals continuing visibly across the image rectangle face (both diagonals of the rectangle appear); the generated frusta only draw the four radiating edges plus rectangle outline plus one vertical midline, so the characteristic crossed-diagonal look of the source base is not reproduced.

plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single horizontal strip in which one camera is repeated five times in a row on a white ground, with thick red arrows between and around the copies. Each camera is a black wireframe viewing frustum in three-quarter view: a solid black dot marks the projection center at the left, four straight edges spread rightward from it to the corners of a tall rectangle standing for the image plane, and a faint vertical line inside that rectangle marks its midline. All five frusta match in size and orientation, and every one opens toward the right. A red arrow lies on the axis left of the first camera, another sits in each gap between consecutive cameras, and a final one continues past the last camera to the right edge; all arrowheads point right. Because the arrows run in the same direction the frusta face, the strip shows a camera moving straight ahead down its own optical axis, the case in which the sideways velocity components vanish and only the component along the Z-axis is nonzero.

demo_steps.title: The camera strip at rest
demo_steps.narration: Five copies of the same camera stand in a row, each apex on the left and each image plane on the right; all frusta face the same way down one optical axis.

demo_steps.title: Stepping forward
demo_steps.narration: Advance the slider: the active camera slides rightward from copy to copy, following the red arrows. Its orientation never changes — only its distance to the scene.

demo_steps.title: End of the path
demo_steps.narration: At the last copy the camera is nearest the scene. The red arrow continues past it, showing the motion is pure translation along +Z with no rotation and no sideways component.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World axes: +X is screen-right (the common optical axis and direction of travel), +Y screen-up, +Z the receding three-quarter diagonal. One camera frustum: apex (projection center) at local origin, drawn as a black sphere of radius 0.10; image rectangle at x = +1.30, sized 1.60 (Y, tall) x 1.00 (Z, deep) so it reads clearly taller than wide, exactly as in the source. Four black edges of tube radius ~0.02 connect the apex to the rectangle's four corners; the rectangle's own four edges are the same weight. A single faint grey (#808080) vertical line of the same radius runs top-to-bottom at the rectangle's mid-depth (z = 0). Five identical, unscaled copies with apexes at x = 0, 3.2, 6.4, 9.6, 12.8, all y = z = 0, all opening toward +X — no size taper of any kind between copies. Red motion arrows (#FF0000, shaft radius 0.075, conical head length 0.35, head radius 0.17) lie exactly on the y=z=0 axis, all pointing +X: one entering from x = -2.4 to -0.25 (just before the first apex), one in each of the four gaps spanning from just right of a rectangle (x ≈ previous apex + 1.45) to just left of the next apex (next apex - 0.25), and a final one from x = 14.3 out to x = 16.6 past the last camera. Background white; wireframe black #000000. Flow-field view: the same image rectangle drawn front-on (1.60 tall x 1.20 wide on screen), a 5x5 grid of projected scene points, and red arrows at each point along the radial direction from the image center, with magnitude |v| = |p| * (Tz / Z) so the vector length grows linearly with distance from the center and vanishes exactly at the focus of expansion at the rectangle's midline center. Image-plane velocity model: u = (-Tx + x*Tz)/Z, v = (-Ty + y*Tz)/Z with Tx = Ty = 0, Tz > 0, Z ≈ 6 world units to the scene.
interactionPlan.notes: Build one frustum as a reusable THREE.Group (sphere apex + 8 cylinder/TubeGeometry edges + grey midline) and instance it five times so all copies are provably identical. Use MeshBasicMaterial or thick LineSegments (Line2/LineMaterial with linewidth ~3px) for the crisp constant-width black wireframe look of the source. Red arrows via ArrowHelper replacements built from a cylinder shaft + cone head so their thickness is world-space and consistent. The slider and animation drive the same underlying t parameter (0-4 in copy units); the animation just auto-advances t and loops back. On toggle to the flow-field view, cross-fade: dolly the camera to a front-on orthographic look at a single image rectangle, hide the strip, and fade in the radial arrow field, recomputing arrow lengths from the current t (closer scene = longer vectors). Keep an orthographic-feeling axonometric camera (OrthographicCamera or a long-focal PerspectiveCamera) so the five copies do not perspectively shrink toward the right.  Orbit via OrbitControls with damping, target at the strip center (x ≈ 6.4).

- Animation for advancing the camera copies along their optical axis; the frustum moves straight through the scene while projected points expand from the image center, linking forward Z translation to radial optical flow.
- Slider for time along the forward path; the active camera position and red direction arrows update together, showing that orientation stays fixed while depth to the scene changes.

discrepancies: Frusta are drawn noticeably smaller relative to the connecting red arrows than in the source, where each camera pyramid is large and the arrows are short interstitial links; the generated strip reads as thin wireframes strung along long arrows.

The row of apexes drifts slightly downward toward the right (apex y falls from ~372 to ~392 px) instead of lying on one strictly level horizontal axis as in the source; also the frusta appear to grow/shrink subtly with depth shear.
The grey image-plane midline that is clearly visible in every source frustum is almost invisible at the rendered scale (radius 0.022 grey cylinder behind the black edges).

Labels ('optical axis — direction of travel', 'T = (0,0,T_z)', 'projection centre C', 'image plane') and the separate flow-field panel are additions not present in the source figure — pedagogically useful but they change the visual character of an otherwise annotation-free diagram.

The near/far vertical edges of the image rectangle are oriented such that the depth of the rectangle recedes down-right, whereas the source's rectangles clearly recede up-right, giving a slightly different oblique read of each pyramid.
